text: When David's time to die drew near, he charged his son Solomon:
"I am going the way of all the earth. Be strong, and show yourself a man.

Keep the charge of the LORD your God: walk in his ways, and keep his statutes, his commandments, his ordinances, and his testimonies, as it is written in the Law of Moses, so that you may prosper in everything you do and everywhere you turn.

Do this so that the LORD may fulfill the promise he made concerning me: 'If your sons watch their way and walk faithfully before me with all their heart and with all their soul, you will never lack a man on the throne of Israel.'

versions.text: Then the LORD will fulfill the promise he made concerning me: 'If your sons watch their way and walk faithfully before me with all their heart and with all their soul, you will never lack a man on the throne of Israel.'
versions.explanation: The Hebrew לְמַעַן expresses purpose, linking obedience in verse 3 with the fulfillment of the promise. "Then the LORD will fulfill" flattens this into a simple prediction; a purpose clause preserves the connective force while still reading smoothly aloud.

versions.text: Do this so that the LORD may fulfill the promise he made concerning me:
versions.explanation: The entire content of the LORD's promise has been dropped. The Hebrew continues with the conditional clause (אִם־יִשְׁמְרוּ בָנֶיךָ אֶת־דַּרְכָּם... בְּכָל־לְבָבָם וּבְכָל־נַפְשָׁם) and its apodosis (לֹא־יִכָּרֵת לְךָ אִישׁ מֵעַל כִּסֵּא יִשְׂרָאֵל). The introductory colon in the current text points to a quotation that is no longer there, leaving the verse incomplete. The intentional purpose-clause opening ("Do this so that...") is retained.

text: You also know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me—what he did to the two commanders of Israel's armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He killed them, shedding the blood of war in a time of peace, and he put the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet.
Act with the wisdom you have, and do not let his gray head go down to the grave in peace.
But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for they stood by me when I fled from your brother Absalom.

And there is with you Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim. He cursed me with a bitter curse the day I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, 'I will not put you to death by the sword.'
Now do not let him go unpunished. You are a wise man; you will know what to do to him. Bring his gray head down to the grave in blood."
Then David slept with his fathers and was buried in the City of David.
David reigned over Israel forty years: seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
So Solomon sat on the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established.
Now Adonijah son of Haggith came to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother. She asked, "Do you come in peace?" "In peace," he said.
Then he added, "I have something to say to you." "Speak," she said.
He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel looked to me as king. But the kingdom has turned about and gone to my brother, for it came to him from the LORD.
Now I have one request to make of you; do not refuse me." "Speak," she said.
He said, "Please ask King Solomon—he will not refuse you—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife."
"Very well," Bathsheba said, "I will speak to the king for you."

So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him for Adonijah. The king rose to meet her and bowed to her; then he sat down on his throne and had a throne brought for the king's mother, and she sat at his right hand.
She said, "I have one small request to make of you; do not refuse me." The king answered, "Ask, my mother; I will not refuse you."
So she said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to your brother Adonijah as his wife."

King Solomon answered his mother, "And why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask the kingdom for him as well—he is my older brother—yes, for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab son of Zeruiah!"
Then King Solomon swore by the LORD: "May God do so to me and more also, if Adonijah has not spoken this word at the cost of his life!
Now therefore, as the LORD lives, who has established me and seated me on the throne of my father David and who has made me a house as he promised—today Adonijah shall be put to death!"
So King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who struck Adonijah down, and he died.

To Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your own fields. You deserve to die, but I will not put you to death now, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before my father David and shared in all my father's hardships."
So Solomon removed Abiathar from serving as priest to the LORD, fulfilling the word the LORD had spoken at Shiloh concerning the house of Eli.
When the news reached Joab—who had sided with Adonijah, though he had not sided with Absalom—he fled to the tent of the LORD and took hold of the horns of the altar.
King Solomon was told that Joab had fled to the tent of the LORD and was there beside the altar. So Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada with the order, "Go, strike him down."

Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to Joab, "The king says, 'Come out!'" But he answered, "No, I will die here." Benaiah brought word back to the king: "This is what Joab said, and this is how he answered me."

versions.text: Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to him, "The king says, 'Come out!'" But he answered, "No, I will die here." Benaiah brought word back to the king: "This is what Joab said, and this is how he answered me."
versions.explanation: In oral reading, "said to him" is ambiguous because Benaiah is the nearest named subject. Naming Joab explicitly (as the Hebrew pronoun clearly intends) removes the confusion without adding content.

versions.text: Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to Joab, "The king says, 'Come out!'" But he answered, "No, I will die here."
versions.explanation: The final clause of the verse has been lost: וַיָּשֶׁב בְּנָיָהוּ אֶת־הַמֶּלֶךְ דָּבָר לֵאמֹר כֹּה־דִבֶּר יוֹאָב וְכֹה עָנָנִי, Benaiah's report back to the king. Without it the narrative jumps to Solomon's reply in verse 31 with no reported speech to answer. The intentional clarification "said to Joab" is kept.

text: The king said to him, "Do as he says. Strike him down and bury him, and so remove from me and from my father's house the innocent blood that Joab shed.

The LORD will bring Joab's blood back on his own head, because he struck down two men more righteous and better than himself and killed them with the sword, without my father David's knowledge: Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel's army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah's army.

versions.text: The LORD will bring his blood back on his own head, because he struck down two men more righteous and better than himself and killed them with the sword, without my father David's knowledge: Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel's army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah's army.
versions.explanation: For oral reading, the opening "his blood ... his own head" leaves the referent unclear, especially since two other men are named later in the verse. Naming Joab at the start (as the next verse does) removes the ambiguity without adding content.

text: Their blood will come back on the head of Joab and on the head of his descendants forever; but for David and his descendants, his house and his throne, there will be peace from the LORD forevermore."
So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, struck Joab down, and put him to death; and he was buried at his own house in the wilderness.
The king put Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army in his place, and he put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.
Then the king summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there; do not go out from there to anywhere at all.
On the day you leave and cross the Kidron Valley, know for certain that you will die; your blood will be on your own head."
Shimei answered the king, "The sentence is fair. As my lord the king has said, so your servant will do." And Shimei lived in Jerusalem a long time.
But at the end of three years, two of Shimei's slaves ran away to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath, and Shimei was told, "Your slaves are in Gath."
So Shimei got up, saddled his donkey, and went to Achish at Gath to look for his slaves; he went and brought them back from Gath.
When Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and returned,

the king summoned Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD and warn you, 'On the day you leave and go anywhere at all, know for certain that you will die'? And you said to me, 'The sentence is fair; I will obey.'
Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the command I laid on you?"
The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your own heart all the evil you did to my father David. So the LORD will bring your evil back on your own head.

versions.text: The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your own heart all the evil you did to my father David. Now the LORD brings your evil back on your own head.
versions.explanation: The verb וְהֵשִׁיב is a waw-consecutive perfect with future force, parallel to the identical construction in verse 32 (rendered there as "will bring"). The present tense "brings" breaks that parallel and weakens the declarative force of the pronouncement.

text: But King Solomon will be blessed, and David's throne will be established before the LORD forever."
Then the king gave the order to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who went out and struck Shimei down, and he died. So the kingdom was firmly established in Solomon's hand.
